sections.section_title: Clinical Approach to Post–Cardiac Surgery Thrombocytopenia and Thrombosis
sections.description: Framework to evaluate platelet count declines and thrombotic events after cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB), with emphasis on recognizing autoimmune heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (aHIT) and initiating time-sensitive therapy.
key_points: Differentiate expected CPB-related thrombocytopenia (early, modest, transient) from HIT/aHIT (often biphasic or progressive with new thrombosis).
Typical HIT after cardiac surgery manifests between POD5–10; onset before POD5 suggests preoperative heparin exposure.

Use a structured pretest probability tool (e.g., 4Ts), while recognizing limitations in post-CPB patients; intermediate/high probability warrants immediate non-heparin anticoagulation without waiting for confirmatory testing.
Assess for and promptly image suspected thrombotic complications (e.g., ischemic stroke) even with delirium or subtle signs.
Stop all heparin exposures, including LMWH prophylaxis and heparin flushes, when HIT/aHIT is suspected.
Order PF4/polyanion immunoassay and a functional platelet activation test in parallel; engage a reference laboratory early for atypical results.

sections.section_title: Pathophysiology: From Classic HIT to Autoimmune HIT
sections.description: Mechanistic basis of HIT and the distinct immunobiology of aHIT, including heparin-independent platelet activation and severe hypercoagulability.
key_points: Classic HIT: IgG antibodies target PF4–heparin complexes, form immune complexes, and activate platelets via FcγRIIa clustering; high-dose heparin disrupts complexes and suppresses activation.

Autoimmune HIT (aHIT): Subset in which anti-PF4 antibodies can activate platelets in the absence of heparin; clinical phenotypes include delayed-onset, persisting, severe thrombocytopenia, and heparin-independent activation.

Heparin-independent activation likely reflects antibodies targeting PF4 on platelet/monocyte surfaces and/or interaction with endogenous polyanions; may involve complement and cellular cross-talk, amplifying thrombin generation.
Partial resistance to FcγRIIa blockade (e.g., incomplete inhibition by IV.3) can occur with highly potent aHIT antibodies and should not be misinterpreted as ruling out HIT.

aHIT is strongly prothrombotic (relative risk for thrombosis markedly increased) and may present with arterial events (e.g., stroke) and laboratory evidence of consumptive coagulopathy (falling fibrinogen, rising D-dimer, schistocytes).
Antibody dynamics evolve over weeks to months: early heparin-independent activation can wane to a more classic heparin-dependent profile as titers decline.

sections.section_title: Differential Diagnosis of Early Postoperative Thrombocytopenia After CPB
sections.description: Systematic differential for significant platelet count declines after cardiac surgery, and features that favor HIT/aHIT in this setting.
key_points: Common non-immune causes: CPB-related dilution/consumption, surgical blood loss, hemodilution, sequestration; these typically produce modest early declines with stabilization or recovery by POD3–4.
Critical illness/shock, infection/sepsis, disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC): consider with abnormal vitals, organ dysfunction, prolonged PT/aPTT, hypofibrinogenemia.

Immune-mediated thrombocytopenias: classic HIT/aHIT; drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia (temporal relationship often too late post-op; consider culprit drugs); post-transfusion purpura (requires transfusion exposure).
Thrombotic microangiopathies (TTP/HUS): look for MAHA (schistocytes, low haptoglobin, elevated LDH), neurologic/renal dysfunction; ADAMTS13 testing if suspected.
Device-related platelet consumption (IABP, ECMO), mechanical hemolysis, and pseudo-thrombocytopenia (clumping) should be excluded.

Clues favoring aHIT: new thrombosis (e.g., ischemic stroke), strong-positive PF4 ELISA, functional assay activation at 0 U/mL heparin with inhibition at supratherapeutic heparin, early onset tied to recent preoperative heparin exposure.

sections.section_title: Diagnostic Workup and Interpretation of HIT/aHIT Testing
sections.description: Evidence-based testing strategy, interpretation of immunoassays and functional assays, and how to recognize aHIT-specific patterns.
key_points: Apply pretest probability (4Ts) to guide testing and immediate management; avoid overreliance on timing alone in post-CPB patients.
PF4/polyanion ELISA: IgG-specific assays preferred; higher optical density strongly correlates with platelet-activating antibodies and thrombosis risk.
Functional assays: Serotonin-release assay (SRA) or HIPA confirm pathogenicity. Typical HIT shows strong release at therapeutic heparin, suppression at high heparin (e.g., 100 U/mL).
aHIT hallmark: platelet activation in the absence of heparin (0 U/mL) with retention of high-heparin inhibition; partial resistance to FcγRIIa blockade (IV.3) can occur in severe aHIT.
When SRA is indeterminate or clinical–laboratory discordance exists, request PF4-enhanced SRA or flow-based P-selectin expression assay to increase sensitivity for aHIT.
Trend ancillary markers of coagulopathy (fibrinogen down, D-dimer up, schistocytes) as severity surrogates and to gauge response to therapy.
Document recent heparin exposures (e.g., preoperative catheterization) that can explain early-onset HIT.

sections.section_title: Management of HIT and Autoimmune HIT After Cardiac Surgery
sections.description: Immediate and definitive therapy for HIT/aHIT, selection and dosing of non-heparin anticoagulants, immunomodulation, and monitoring strategies.
key_points: Immediate steps: discontinue all forms of heparin/LMWH (including flushes), and start a non-heparin anticoagulant even with severe thrombocytopenia or arterial thrombosis.

Anticoagulant options: argatroban (hepatic clearance; aPTT-guided), bivalirudin (renal/enzymatic clearance; preferred in some post-CPB scenarios), fondaparinux (once-daily SC; avoid prophylactic dosing—use therapeutic dosing; renal clearance).

In aHIT with severe hypercoagulability or suboptimal response, add high-dose IVIG (total 1–2 g/kg, often divided over 2–3 days) to block Fcγ receptor–mediated platelet activation; repeat dosing may be required.
Consider antithrombin concentrate if selecting an indirect factor Xa inhibitor (e.g., fondaparinux) and antithrombin levels are low, to optimize anti-Xa effect.
Use laboratory trends (platelet count up, D-dimer down, fibrinogen stabilizing/rising) to assess control; persistent consumption suggests refractory disease and need to adjust therapy.
Avoid platelet transfusions unless life-threatening bleeding or urgent procedures; transfusion can exacerbate thrombosis in active HIT.

Warfarin is contraindicated in acute HIT; initiate only after platelet recovery (typically ≥150 × 10^9/L) with overlap; direct oral anticoagulants (e.g., apixaban) are effective options for transition once stable.
Treat confirmed thrombosis for at least 3 months; for isolated HIT without thrombosis, treat generally 4–6 weeks. Tailor duration to comorbid indications (e.g., atrial fibrillation).
Special situations: for future cardiac surgery, avoid heparin if possible (e.g., bivalirudin for CPB); if heparin unavoidable, consider timing after antibody waning with expert consultation.

sections.description: Expected clinical course, antibody kinetics, prevention of recurrence, and key practice points distilled from the case.
key_points: Platelet recovery may be delayed in aHIT despite therapy; antibodies often persist for weeks to months, and functional assay profiles can evolve from heparin-independent to heparin-dependent as titers fall.
Thrombotic risk remains elevated until platelet recovery and laboratory markers improve; maintain therapeutic anticoagulation unless contraindicated.
Document a heparin allergy and educate the patient and care teams to avoid all heparin products (including LMWH and heparin-bonded catheters).
Early-onset HIT after cardiac surgery is a red flag for recent preoperative heparin exposure—even small doses (e.g., during diagnostic catheterization).
Prophylactic-dose fondaparinux is inadequate for suspected HIT; use therapeutic dosing. Consider antithrombin supplementation if levels are low and an indirect Xa inhibitor is chosen.
Partial inhibition by FcγRIIa-blocking antibodies in functional assays does not exclude aHIT; seek PF4-enhanced testing at experienced laboratories.
Track fibrinogen and D-dimer serially as pragmatic markers of consumptive coagulopathy and treatment efficacy.
Arterial thrombosis, including ischemic stroke, can complicate aHIT; coordinate hematology and neurology care to balance anticoagulation and bleeding risk.
Overall prognosis is favorable with prompt recognition, heparin cessation, appropriate alternative anticoagulation, and immunomodulation when indicated.
